feature: per-port `protocol:` inspectability / TLS-pinning passthrough (M5 P1 — #233 + #238 + #239/PR #262, re-run on PR #264's tip)

journeys.rationale: Quietness is a promise too: a firewall that declares nothing unusual must read as ordinary, so that the one time a warning does appear it means something. A surface that decorates every policy trains operators to ignore it.

source.ref: docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-18-m5-p1-inspectability.md — the renderer is silent when a port declares nothing

steps.intent: create a sandbox called plain-fw for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is on and allows just the two hosts api.vendor.example and registry.other.example
steps.expect: the create command finishes without an error

steps.intent: read back what plain-fw's firewall allows and judge whether izba is flagging anything unusual about it
steps.expect: the two hosts and their web ports are listed plainly, with no warning markers about inspection or bypass

journeys.rationale: Declaring an exemption is documented as something you do by editing the sandbox's own policy file and reloading — there is no CLI flag for it. The reload must confirm WHICH file it re-read, so an operator who edited a stray copy is not told 'success' about a file izba never looked at.

source.ref: PR #264 commit 'fix(cli): name the reloaded policy path and warn --follow never exits' (DEEP-2); `izba policy reload` help names the managed file's location

steps.intent: create a sandbox called reload-pin for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall allows the host pinned.vendor.example on port 443, with nothing exempted yet
steps.expect: the sandbox is created with the firewall on

steps.intent: a certificate-pinning client now has to run in reload-pin — change that sandbox's firewall so port 443 of pinned.vendor.example reaches the vendor's own TLS untouched, and make izba pick the change up
steps.expect: izba re-reads the sandbox's settings and tells you exactly which file it read them from

journeys.rationale: The dormant case must be true in the datapath and not merely in the wording: an exemption on a read-only host row is still intercepted, so a pinning client really does see izba's certificate. If the two surfaces say 'not in effect' but the traffic is spliced anyway, the honest wording is the more dangerous bug.

source.ref: CLAUDE.md: 'router::passthrough_names drops the host and the connection stays terminated at L7, so a pinning client still sees izba's certificate'

steps.intent: create a sandbox called pin-dormant for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is on, restricts the host example.com to read-only access on ports 80 and 443, and nevertheless declares port 443 of that host exempt from interception
steps.expect: the sandbox is created with the read-only restriction and the declared exemption

steps.intent: start pin-dormant and, from inside it, fetch https://example.com/ over TLS
steps.expect: the fetch completes from inside the sandbox

steps.intent: ask izba's connection log for that sandbox what it actually did with that connection, and compare it with what the firewall report claims about that port
steps.expect: the log shows the connection being inspected at the HTTP layer, matching the report's claim that the exemption is not in effect

journeys.rationale: An exemption declared for one host must not un-inspect the same port for every other host that is allowed on it. This is the difference between a per-host, per-port exemption and a global hole punched in inspection.

source.ref: CLAUDE.md: 'an explicit `tcp` entry does not remove its own port from the inspected set'; InspectionTable's per-host passthrough set vs its policy-global inspected port set

steps.intent: create a sandbox called two-hosts for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is on and allows two hosts on ports 80 and 443 — example.com, whose port 443 is exempt from interception for a certificate-pinning client, and example.net, which gets no such exemption
steps.expect: the sandbox is created with the exemption on one host only

steps.intent: start two-hosts and, from inside it, fetch https://example.net/ over TLS
steps.expect: the fetch completes from inside the sandbox

steps.intent: ask izba's connection log what it did with the connection to the host you did NOT exempt
steps.expect: that host's traffic on port 443 was still inspected at the HTTP layer — the other host's exemption did not extend to it

journeys.rationale: The exemption is bound to the name izba's OWN resolver answered for this sandbox, never to an address the guest brought in from somewhere else. A client that dials such an address must not inherit the opaque splice: the connection is still authorized by name, but it is terminated and inspected at the HTTP layer like any other — otherwise anything inside the sandbox could claim the exemption by supplying its own address.

source.ref: CLAUDE.md: 'only over the candidate list router::passthrough_names derives from DNS-snoop'; plan DP-2 ('no snoop record ⇒ no passthrough') — which promises the flow is NOT spliced, not that it is denied

steps.intent: create a sandbox called raw-addr for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is on, allows the host example.com on ports 80 and 443, and exempts port 443 of that host from interception
steps.expect: the sandbox is created with that exempt port

steps.intent: look up one of example.com's numeric IPv4 addresses on your own machine (the sandbox itself has no IPv6 route), then start raw-addr and, from inside it, open a TLS connection to https://example.com/ that goes straight to that numeric address — the sandbox must not ask izba to resolve the name for itself, while the request still presents the site's name to the server it reaches
steps.expect: the request leaves from inside the sandbox and the site answers it

steps.intent: ask izba's connection log what it did with that attempt
steps.expect: the connection to that host on port 443 was allowed, but it was inspected at the HTTP layer rather than passed through untouched — the exemption did not carry over to an address izba never resolved for this sandbox

journeys.rationale: Egress settings are a live-class change: adding an exemption to a running sandbox and reloading must take effect on the next connection without stopping anything. A user who has to restart loses their session for a firewall tweak.

source.ref: `izba policy reload` help: 'Re-read a sandbox's policy.yaml and apply it to new connections (no restart)'

steps.intent: create and start a sandbox called live-pin for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is on and allows the host example.com on ports 80 and 443, with nothing exempted, and confirm from inside it that https://example.com/ can be fetched
steps.expect: the sandbox is running and the fetch works

steps.intent: without stopping the sandbox, change live-pin's firewall so port 443 of example.com now reaches the site's own TLS untouched, and make izba apply it
steps.expect: izba applies the change to the running sandbox and says it takes effect on new connections

steps.intent: fetch https://example.com/ from inside the still-running sandbox again, then ask izba's connection log what it did with THAT connection
steps.expect: the newer connection was passed through rather than inspected, without the sandbox ever having been restarted

journeys.rationale: Seeding the allow-list from what a sandbox actually reached goes through the same mutator as a manual grant, so it too must append plain ports and must not disturb an existing exemption. This mutator is the one a user is least likely to inspect afterwards.

source.ref: CLAUDE.md: 'EgressPolicyConfig::allow (and every other mutator, for every caller — CLI, GUI, observed-traffic seeding) appends a port that structurally cannot inherit a sibling port's hatch'

steps.intent: create and start a sandbox called seeded for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is on, allows the host example.com on ports 80 and 443 with port 443 exempt from interception, and also allows example.net; from inside it fetch both https://example.com/ and https://example.net/
steps.expect: the sandbox is running and both fetches complete

steps.intent: now have izba build seeded's allow-list up from the traffic it has actually been permitting, so the list reflects real usage
steps.expect: izba reports how many observed endpoints it added and reloads the sandbox's settings

steps.intent: read back seeded's firewall and check what happened to the exempt port and to anything newly added
steps.expect: the exemption is still attached to the port it was declared on, and nothing that was added from observed traffic is exempt

journeys.rationale: The desktop editor's save path has no weakening review in front of it, so renaming a host that carries an exemption would move that exemption onto a host nobody declared one for. The refusal must survive a real save and a re-read, not merely look refused on screen — so this journey makes a legitimate edit alongside the refused one, and grades the saved settings.

source.ref: PR #262 'The decision (AC 4)': relocation and activation are both refused in the reducer

seed_files.izba.yml:
apiVersion: izba.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Sandbox
spec:
  image: alpine:3.20
  egress:
    enforce: true
    allow:
      - host: pinned.vendor.example
        ports:
          - 80
          - port: 443
            protocol: tcp
      - host: api.vendor.example
        ports:
          - 443

steps.intent: type {workspace} into the Workspace field, 'gui-pin5' into the Name field, and 'alpine:3.20' into the Image field, then click Create to create a new sandbox from this workspace
steps.expect: the create finishes without an error banner and a sandbox named gui-pin5 appears in the sandbox list

steps.intent: open gui-pin5's detail view, go to the view listing the hosts it may reach, and try to change the vendor host that carries the exempt port so that it reads moved.vendor.example instead; give the view a moment to finish loading, looking again if it is not ready yet, before reading or changing anything
steps.expect: what the host field does with the typing is visible in the field itself, and the row shows a message next to it

steps.intent: while you are here, also add port 8080 to the OTHER host row — the one with no exempt port — and then save the whole thing back to the sandbox
steps.expect: the save completes and the footer reports the settings were written

steps.intent: re-read the saved settings for gui-pin5 and check which hosts are there and where the exemption ended up; give the view a moment to finish loading, looking again if it is not ready yet, before reading or changing anything
steps.expect: the vendor host still has its original name and still carries the exemption on the same port; the rename did not take

journeys.rationale: The escape valve: the row's restrictions exist only because of the exempt port, so removing that port must lift them together. Otherwise a user who genuinely wants to rename or re-open a host is stuck with no route out inside the app.

source.ref: PR #262: 'Removing the pinned port is the escape valve for BOTH the Host lock and the Access-widening refusal'
